title: Coaching Cut #50: Skipping Success Criteria Leadership Cognitive Coaching
author: Cognitive Coaching
summary: This installment of the Cognitive Coaching series addresses a specific pitfall in instructional coaching: the modelling step frequently fails not because the model is poor but because the coach has neglected to prime the coachee with explicit success criteria before the demonstration begins. Without that priming, the coachee watches everything and focuses on nothing, defaulting to whatever surface features of the technique are most visually prominent rather than the subtler elements that actually produce learning gains. The proposed solution is structural: wrap success criteria around the model on all three sides -- naming what to watch for before the model, ensuring those criteria are unmissable during it, and then asking the coachee to explain why each criterion matters for learning after. The before-and-after contrast demonstrates that the model itself need not change at all; what changes is the cognitive frame the coachee brings to observing it. This structural adjustment converts a demonstration from a passive visual experience into a guided analytical encounter, which is the precondition for the coachee subsequently rehearsing and implementing the practice with genuine fidelity.
points: * Modelling without pre-stated success criteria is the most common invisible failure in instructional coaching: the coach delivers a technically correct model, but the coachee's attention lands on surface features rather than the specific moves that make the technique work -- and subsequent rehearsal reproduces a weakened version. * 'Watch carefully and tell me what you think' sounds like an invitation to attend but is functionally a vague instruction -- it produces diffuse observation rather than focused analysis, and diffuse observation misses precisely the subtle success criteria that distinguish effective from ineffective execution. * The fix is a three-step envelope: before the model, name specifically what to look for (especially anything subtle); during, make those criteria unmissable; after, ask the coachee to explain why each criterion matters for learning -- moving from seeing to understanding. * The before/after contrast demonstrates a counterintuitive principle: the quality of what the coachee learns from a model is determined not by the model's content but by the cognitive frame the coach creates around it. * Skipping success criteria means the coachee implements a partial version of the practice, lacks the analytical vocabulary to notice the deficit, and neither coach nor coachee can easily diagnose why the technique is not producing the expected effect on learning.
quotes: Skipping the success criteria is where you model without priming your teacher for what they are about to see. When a coach says, 'I'm going to model this for you, so watch carefully and tell me what you think,' it Page 1 feels like enough. It sounds like an invitation to pay attention. But it's actually a vague instruction.

The coachee is watching everything and focusing on nothing. Their attention lands on whatever is most obvious, the surface features of the technique. The subtler success criteria -- the ones that actually make the practice work -- go unnoticed.

The result is that the coachee rehearses and implements a partial version of the practice. It doesn't have the intended effect on learning, and neither coach nor coachee can easily see why because they never pinned down and verbalised the success criteria that made the technique work.

We wrap the success criteria around the model: before, during, and after. Before the model, we tell the coachee exactly what to watch for. Not everything, just the criteria that matter most, especially any that are subtle or easy to miss.

After the model, we spotlight the key criteria and ask the coachee to explain why they matter for learning. This is where understanding is built. It's not enough that they saw it. They need to understand why it works.
In the clip below, the coach delivers the exact same model: same words, same pauses, same checks. The only difference is what the coach does before and after." Page 2
